questions.question: Why is chunking strategy as important as the embedding model in RAG?
options: Chunking shrinks the embedding model's own parameter count, which is why smaller chunks always run faster at inference time
Chunking is a hard requirement of vector index libraries like FAISS, not an optional quality lever
Smaller chunks always train faster, since the embedding model has fewer tokens to process per document
Chunk boundaries determine whether the answer is even retrievable at all; bad chunks defeat any embedding model
questions.explanation: Vectara's 2025 study showed chunking quality matches or exceeds embedding-model impact on retrieval quality.

questions.question: What does LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter try in order?
options: Try splitting on paragraph breaks first, then newlines, then sentence boundaries, then spaces as a last resort
Always split at a fixed character position N, regardless of where sentences or paragraphs fall
Split directly on the tokenizer's own token IDs, ignoring character-level structure like punctuation marks entirely
Split on whitespace characters only, treating every other separator as part of the chunk content
questions.explanation: Recursive splitting falls back through paragraph -> newline -> sentence -> space to preserve structure.

questions.question: Why does the parent-document pattern improve answer quality?
options: It removes the need for embeddings entirely by matching parent documents with keyword search alone
It avoids tokenization overhead by operating directly on raw document bytes instead of chunked text
Small child chunks give precise retrieval; the larger parent block returned instead preserves surrounding context
It uses noticeably fewer GPU cycles than single-level chunking because parent blocks skip re-embedding, because one plausible output is sufficient production evidence
questions.explanation: Retrieve by small child chunks for precision, then expand to the parent for context.

questions.question: What does Anthropic's 'contextual retrieval' add to each chunk before indexing?
options: A part-of-speech tag for the chunk's dominant grammatical structure, used to filter irrelevant matches
An LLM-generated summary placing the chunk in the document's overall context, such as which section it belongs to
A language code identifying which of several supported languages the chunk's text is written in
Randomly sampled noise tokens, used as a regularizer that prevents the retriever from overfitting to exact phrasing
questions.explanation: Contextual retrieval prepends an LLM-written situating summary to each chunk; ~35-50% recall gain.

questions.question: Which 2026 finding contradicts the conventional wisdom about chunk overlap?
options: Empirical 2026 benchmarks show overlap often provides zero measurable retrieval benefit while inflating index size
Chunk overlap is a hard architectural requirement for BM25 to score documents correctly, unlike dense retrieval — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
Overlap only improves results when combined with contextual retrieval, and does nothing on its own
The optimal overlap percentage was found to be exactly 50% of the chunk size across all query types
questions.explanation: Newer studies (SPLADE+Mistral on NQ) show chunk overlap rarely helps and inflates index size.

questions.question: Which chunk size does NVIDIA's 2026 benchmark associate with factoid queries?
options: About 64 tokens, small enough that only a single sentence fragment ever fits in one chunk
1024-2048 tokens, the size the benchmark recommends for whole-section comprehension queries instead
512-1024 tokens, the size the benchmark recommends for analytical or multi-hop queries instead
Roughly 256-512 tokens, big enough to contain the answer plus local context without excess noise
questions.explanation: Factoid queries benefit from smaller chunks (256-512 tokens) that concentrate the answer signal.
